nameStory: The bar-tailed godwit gets its name from the distinctive barred pattern across its tail feathers, which shows up beautifully when the bird spreads its tail in flight. The 'godwit' part of the name comes from an old English word that mimics the bird's loud, piercing call - something like 'god-wit, god-wit!' that carries across mudflats and marshes.
description: The bar-tailed godwit is a large, elegant shorebird about the size of a crow, with incredibly long legs and a distinctive long, slightly upturned bill. During breeding season, these birds sport gorgeous rusty-red plumage on their head and chest, while in winter they're more subdued gray-brown. They're champion long-distance migrants, traveling thousands of miles between their Arctic breeding grounds and warmer coastal wintering areas. In New England, they're quite rare visitors, with only about 10 sightings recorded.

idTips.label: Long upturned bill
idTips.description: The bill curves slightly upward and is about twice the length of the head - perfect for probing deep into mud for worms and shellfish

idTips.label: Barred tail pattern
idTips.description: When flying or displaying, look for the distinctive black and white striped pattern across the tail feathers that gives this bird its name

idTips.label: Rusty breeding plumage
idTips.description: In spring and early summer, the head, neck, and chest turn a beautiful brick-red or cinnamon color that's unmistakable

idTips.label: Long pink-orange legs
idTips.description: The legs extend well beyond the tail in flight and have a distinctive salmon-pink to orange color

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: Noticeably larger than most sandpipers - about crow-sized with a robust, sturdy build

idTips.label: Probing feeding behavior
idTips.description: Watch for the characteristic deep probing motion as they thrust their long bills far into mudflats, often burying their heads completely

habitat: In New England, bar-tailed godwits are extremely rare visitors to coastal mudflats, salt marshes, and tidal estuaries, particularly during migration periods. Look for them on expansive muddy areas at low tide where they can probe for marine worms and shellfish. They prefer open shoreline habitats with minimal vegetation where they have clear sightlines for spotting predators.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare spring migrants may appear in breeding plumage with bright rusty-red head and chest coloring. Peak migration would be late April through May.
seasonality.summer: Virtually absent from New England during summer months as they breed in the far Arctic tundra.
seasonality.fall: Slightly more likely than spring, with birds in duller gray-brown winter plumage appearing from August through October during southward migration.
seasonality.winter: Not expected in New England winters as these birds migrate to much warmer coastal areas in the Southern Hemisphere.

funFact: Bar-tailed godwits hold the world record for the longest non-stop flight of any bird - some fly over 7,000 miles from Alaska to New Zealand without stopping to eat, drink, or rest, a journey that takes over a week of continuous flying!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the more common Hudsonian Godwit, but bar-tailed godwits have a slightly upturned bill (Hudsonian bills are straight), and lack the bold white wing stripe that Hudsonians flash in flight. Remember: 'bar-tailed bends up' - the bill curves upward.
contextualKnowledge: Bar-tailed godwits are so rare in New England that any sighting would be considered a significant birding event worth reporting to local birding communities and databases. Most New England birders go their entire lives without seeing one locally.
compareHints: Compared to the Hudsonian Godwit (the most similar species), bar-tailed godwits have that distinctive upturned bill and lack the bold white wing patches. Unlike the larger Marbled Godwit, bar-tails show much more contrast between their breeding and non-breeding plumages, and have that telltale barred tail pattern instead of the marbled appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to the Marbled Godwit (the other godwit regularly seen in New England), Hudsonian Godwits are smaller with a straighter bill and completely different wing pattern in flight.
Among the godwits, Marbled Godwits are the largest and show the most consistent warm brown coloration throughout the year.
Among the godwits, Black-tailed is the only one with that distinctive white wingbar and the black-on-white tail pattern.
